cases.a: marry while young and build a household together
cases.b: complete extended education and secure earnings before marrying
cases.old: Young adults can usually earn an independent living after relatively short training. A couple can begin a household while still gaining experience and possessions.
cases.new: Desirable work requires many years of education. Few young adults can earn enough for secure housing until they finish their training.
cases.explanation: long training and insecure early earnings made waiting more practical
cases.institution: Employers and educational establishments now organize the usual path to a career around many years of training before financial independence

cases.topic: How closely to direct children's time
cases.a: let children spend much of their free time in independent play with ordinary neighborhood supervision
cases.b: personally organize and supervise much of children's free time
cases.old: Children commonly play in neighborhood groups; formal admissions and examinations do not depend much on organized activities during childhood.
cases.new: Access to desirable education increasingly depends on competitive examinations and childhood accomplishments; supervised coaching substantially improves results.
cases.explanation: organized coaching gives children an advantage in increasingly competitive examinations
cases.institution: Schools and clubs give favorable consideration to documented supervised achievements

cases.a: remain with one employer for most of a working life
cases.b: change employers when the move improves earnings or skills
cases.old: Long service brings unusually reliable employment and steadily increasing pay; a worker's experience is difficult to use elsewhere.
cases.new: Skills transfer readily between employers, long service brings little security, and competing firms can offer much better prospects.
cases.explanation: portable skills and insecure tenure make changing employers useful
cases.institution: Professional associations and employment arrangements recognize qualifications and benefits when employees change firms

cases.a: have one married adult concentrate on paid work and the other on household care
cases.b: have both married adults earn wages and divide household care
cases.old: Domestic tasks require much time, childcare beyond the household is scarce, and a second wage earner usually has limited opportunities.
cases.new: Reliable childcare and labor-saving household equipment are inexpensive, and both adults have good chances for paid employment.
cases.explanation: improvements in childcare and work opportunities make a shared arrangement worthwhile
cases.institution: Employers and childcare services provide practical support for families in which both adults work

cases.a: remain near relatives and exchange practical help with them
cases.b: move farther away for better opportunities and establish new networks
cases.old: Travel and communication are expensive; insurance is uncertain and family members nearby provide most help in emergencies.
cases.new: Travel and long-distance communication are inexpensive, insurance is dependable, and work in distant towns pays substantially more.
cases.explanation: insurance and reliable travel make leaving relatives less hazardous
cases.institution: Employment benefits, insurance, and qualifications remain valid when residents move to other towns

cases.topic: How to respond to a serious public insult or injury
cases.a: personally retaliate when seriously wronged so that others know one will not be intimidated
cases.b: seek impartial mediation or a court ruling rather than retaliate
cases.old: Courts seldom enforce judgments and aggressors often exploit people who do not visibly defend themselves.
cases.new: Courts reliably enforce judgments, prevent repeat attacks, and impose penalties on private retaliation.
cases.explanation: impartial enforcement is safer and more effective than private retaliation
cases.institution: The courts give rapid redress and impose substantial penalties for private retaliation

cases.a: permit smoking in enclosed rooms during social gatherings
cases.b: keep enclosed common rooms free of smoking while allowing it outdoors
cases.old: There is little generally accepted evidence that tobacco smoke harms people who are not smoking themselves.
cases.new: Repeated and careful investigations have demonstrated serious harm to nonsmokers from breathing tobacco smoke in enclosed rooms.
cases.explanation: evidence of injury to nonsmokers gives a practical reason to keep shared rooms clear
cases.institution: Meeting halls and employers prohibit indoor smoking but provide places to smoke outdoors

cases.a: give much of an occasional surplus to neighbors who presently need help
cases.b: keep substantial private reserves against future shortages
cases.old: Income and food supplies are fairly steady; emergencies rarely strike many households at once and neighbors ordinarily repay one another's help.
cases.new: Income and food shortages are frequent, severe, and shared by many households at once, leaving little help available from neighbors when a crisis comes.
cases.explanation: widespread shortages make reserves safer than relying on reciprocal aid
cases.institution: Savings associations protect private emergency reserves and encourage regular saving

system: You are a thoughtful English-speaking adult whose outlook was formed by life up to 1930. Answer the following request for advice as you see it. The question may describe an imagined society with unfamiliar conditions; accept only the facts it gives. Do not assume you know what really happens after 1930. Write naturally, as you would in a personal letter, not as a survey researcher.
questions: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
